clinician.final_diagnosis: bilateral femoral neck insufficiency fracture caused by heroin-induced osteoporosis
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 55-year-old male with a 30-year history of intravenous heroin addiction presented with bilateral hip pain, claudication, decreased muscle power, general ache, and lower limb soreness for six months. Initial workup revealed elevated alkaline phosphatase, decreased inorganic phosphate, calcium, and 25-(OH)D3 levels. MRI showed bilateral proximal femur insufficiency fractures, sacral ala insufficiency fractures, and multiple band-like lesions in the spine. A DEXA scan confirmed severe osteoporosis (T-score -3.2 spine, -4.0 hips). Further investigation showed normal parathyroid hormone levels and negative fibroblast growth factor 23, ruling out some metabolic bone diseases. However, decreased testosterone levels were noted, consistent with hypogonadism, and a urine screen was positive for morphine, confirming ongoing heroin use. Plain radiographs confirmed bilateral femoral neck insufficiency fractures with varus displacement. The patient underwent bilateral hip hemiarthroplasty. Six months post-operatively, 25-(OH)D3, inorganic phosphate, and calcium levels showed recovery.
